content: Annual ryegrass toxicity (ARGT) refers to the poisoning of livestock caused by a toxin present in annual ryegrass that has been infected by specific bacteria. The toxin is produced by the bacterium Rathayibacter toxicus (previously known as Clavibacter toxicus), which is introduced into the ryegrass by a nematode species called Anguina funesta. The first documented cases of ARGT occurred in the Black Springs region of South Australia during the 1950s, followed by reports in the Gnowangerup area of Western Australia in the 1960s. Since then, the disease has spread extensively, with approximately 40,000 to 60,000 square kilometers of farmland in Western Australia and similar areas in South Australia now affected by the organisms responsible for ARGT. Livestock losses due to ARGT are most commonly observed between October and January, although cases have been recorded as late as April. Efforts to mitigate the risk of ARGT have included the application of herbicides to reduce ryegrass populations. While this approach has been effective in lowering the risk, it has also led to undesirable consequences, such as a rapid decline in pasture productivity and the emergence of herbicide-resistant ryegrass strains. A more recent and promising method of control involves the use of a biological agent known as the twist fungus. This fungus has been shown to effectively reduce the risk of ARGT without necessitating the eradication of ryegrass. The first application of twist fungus inoculum occurred in 1997, and it has since demonstrated significant potential as a sustainable management strategy.
